## Lists

```{webr-r}
# A list can hold mixed, differently-shaped things together
sample_info <- list(
  id = "GSM3119015",
  values = c(12, 18, 9),
  notes = "control group"
)
sample_info$notes
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Why Lists?
A data frame requires every column to be the same length. A list doesn't —
it's the structure R reaches for when things genuinely don't fit a tidy
rectangle, which happens more often than you'd expect once you start working
with real analysis output (model results, nested settings, mixed metadata).
:::

## Base R Subsetting (Just Enough to Read Code)

```{webr-r}
rawc[1, ]                   # entire first row
rawc[, 3]                   # entire third column
rawc[1059, "GSM3119015"]    # one specific cell
rawc$GSM3119015             # a column, by name
```

Conditional subsetting uses the same comparison operators you already know:
`==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, and `%in%`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — You Don't Need to Master This Today
There are several equally valid ways to subset in base R. The goal here is
recognition, not fluency — so that when you see `df[row, col]` or `df$col`
in someone else's script, you're not stopped cold.
:::

## Checking for Missing Values

```{webr-r}
anyNA(rawc)
which(is.na(rawc$GSM3119015))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Zero vs. NA: Not the Same Thing
A `0` means "we measured this, and the value was zero." An `NA` means
"we don't know this value." Replacing a missing value with `0` without
thinking it through can quietly distort every downstream calculation —
averages, totals, and models all treat a fabricated zero as real data.
:::

## Writing Your Own Function

A function has four parts: a **name**, the **arguments** it accepts, a
**body** of code that runs each time it's called, and a **return value** —
the thing it hands back to you.

```{webr-r}
celsius_to_fahrenheit <- function(temp_c) {
  temp_f <- (temp_c * 9/5) + 32
  return(temp_f)
}
celsius_to_fahrenheit(20)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Anatomy of a Function
```
name        <- function(argument1, argument2 = default) {
                 ... body ...
                 return(value)
               }
```
- **Name** — what you'll call it by, same rules as naming any object
- **Arguments** — the inputs; can have defaults, so callers only need to
  supply what's different each time
- **Body** — the code that runs, using the arguments as temporary objects
- **Return value** — the last line evaluated, or an explicit `return()` —
  what the function hands back to whatever called it

This is the **DRY principle** — Don't Repeat Yourself. If you find yourself
copy-pasting the same calculation more than twice, that's the signal to
wrap it in a function instead.
:::

A function's argument doesn't have to be a single number — it can be an
entire data frame. This is closer to what a function looks like in a real
analysis script:

```{webr-r}
flag_low_expression <- function(df, sample_col, min_count = 10) {
  df[[sample_col]] < min_count
}

low_in_sample <- flag_low_expression(rawc, "GSM3119015", min_count = 10)
sum(low_in_sample, na.rm = TRUE)
```

This one function — written once — can now check *any* sample column for
low-count genes just by changing the `sample_col` argument, instead of
retyping the same comparison by hand for every sample.

## `for` Loops

A `for` loop repeats its body once for every element in a sequence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Anatomy of a `for` Loop
```
for (variable in sequence) {
  ... body ...
}
```
- **Sequence** — the collection being stepped through (a vector, a list, a
  set of column names)
- **Loop variable** — takes on one value from the sequence per repetition
- **Body** — runs once per element, using the current value of the loop
  variable
:::

```{webr-r}
for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i^2)
}
```

The same pattern works over column names, not just numbers — useful when
you want to repeat a check across several samples without retyping it:

```{webr-r}
sample_cols <- grep("^GSM", colnames(rawc), value = TRUE)

for (col in sample_cols[1:3]) {
  n_low <- sum(rawc[[col]] < 10, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(col, ":", n_low, "low-count genes\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — When a `for` Loop Isn't the Best Tool
R is built around **vectorized** operations — functions that act on an
entire vector or data frame at once, without an explicit loop. The same
result above can be written as:

```{webr-r}
colSums(rawc[sample_cols[1:3]] < 10, na.rm = TRUE)
```

One line, same answer, and — critically — much faster on a real dataset
with thousands of rows, because the looping happens in compiled C code
under the hood rather than in R itself. A `for` loop isn't wrong, and it's
often easier to read while you're learning. But once you're comfortable,
watch for places where you're looping over rows or columns just to repeat
a simple comparison — that's usually a sign a vectorized function already
exists for the job.
:::

## `if` / `else` Conditionals

An `if`/`else` chain lets a function respond differently depending on the
value it receives — only one branch runs, whichever condition is met first.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Anatomy of `if` / `else`
```
if (condition1) {
  ... runs if condition1 is TRUE ...
} else if (condition2) {
  ... runs if condition1 was FALSE and condition2 is TRUE ...
} else {
  ... runs if nothing above was TRUE ...
}
```
Each `condition` must evaluate to a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`. R checks
them in order and stops at the first one that's `TRUE` — later branches
are skipped entirely, even if they'd also have been `TRUE`.
:::

```{webr-r}
check_value <- function(x) {
  if (x > 0) {
    "positive"
  } else if (x < 0) {
    "negative"
  } else {
    "zero"
  }
}
check_value(-4)
```

The same structure is what you'd reach for to turn a raw number into a
meaningful research label:

```{webr-r}
classify_expression <- function(count) {
  if (is.na(count)) {
    "missing"
  } else if (count == 0) {
    "not detected"
  } else if (count < 10) {
    "low"
  } else {
    "detected"
  }
}

classify_expression(rawc$GSM3119015[1059])  # the NA we found earlier
```

## From the Console to a Script

Everything in this lesson — functions, loops, conditionals — exists to
solve the same underlying problem: **running commands one at a time, by
hand, at the console is not a reliable way to produce research results.**

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — The Hidden Cost of Line-by-Line Execution
It's common to see analysis scripts written as a long sequence of commands,
run one at a time, with the researcher re-running earlier lines by hand
whenever something upstream changes. This works until it doesn't:

- A line gets skipped by accident, and the output looks fine — it's just wrong
- An object gets overwritten mid-analysis, and an earlier result silently
  reflects the wrong data
- Six months later, no one — including you — can tell which lines were
  actually run, in which order, to produce the result in the paper

A script that runs top-to-bottom without manual intervention, and a
function that performs the same check the same way every time it's called,
both exist to remove *you* as a source of inconsistency between one run
and the next. This is what reproducibility means at the level of a single
script, not just a whole project.
:::

## Reading an Error Message (Deliberate Exercise)

```{r}
#| eval: false
mean(FamAges)   # object doesn't exist yet — intentional
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-important"></span> Instructor Note
Let this error sit uncorrected for a beat before explaining. The goal is
normalizing errors as information, not something to panic over — most of
your future debugging time will be spent reading messages like this one.
:::

## Code Tour: A Small, Reproducible QC Check

This combines everything above — a function, wrapped around a loop,
wrapped around a conditional — into something closer to a real quality
check you'd run once, early, in an analysis script. Read it, run it, and
notice that nothing here is new; it's the same three pieces from this
lesson, nested together.

```{webr-r}
qc_report <- function(df, sample_cols, min_count = 10) {
  for (col in sample_cols) {
    n_low   <- sum(df[[col]] < min_count, na.rm = TRUE)
    pct_low <- round(100 * n_low / nrow(df), 1)
    status  <- if (pct_low > 50) "high dropout" else "ok"
    cat(col, ":", pct_low, "% low-count genes —", status, "\n")
  }
}

qc_report(rawc, grep("^GSM", colnames(rawc), value = TRUE)[1:3])
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Why Bother Wrapping This in a Function?
You could run these three lines by hand for every sample column. But
written this way, the check is guaranteed to run identically for every
sample, it's one call away from being reused in your next project, and if
you later decide `min_count` should be 20 instead of 10, you change it in
exactly one place.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** lists, base R subsetting, a function that operates on a
single value and a function that operates on a whole data frame, a `for`
loop (and its vectorized alternative), an `if`/`else` conditional, a
deliberate error, and a small combined QC function.

**Why it matters:** these are the building blocks that let a script adapt
to real data instead of breaking the first time something doesn't match
exactly what you expected — and, just as importantly, that let an analysis
run the same way twice, which is the whole point of reproducibility at the
level of a single script.
